phonemes.desc: Open central vowel [a] with low tone, written without dot below in the lexical form but historically linked to the agánbára ('force') root.
Voiced velar stop [g] followed by open [a] with low tone.
Palatal nasal [ɲ] — like Spanish ñ — plus close back rounded vowel [u] with high tone.

pronunciation.approximation: ah-gah-NYOO — start low on 'ah', stay low on 'gah', then rise sharply to 'NYOO'.

pronunciation.note: Aganjú is Tier 1: the acute accent on ú preserves the high tone of the final syllable, a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. The dot below is absent from the lexical form because the stem vowel is plain /a/, not open /ɔ/ or /ɛ/.

domains.title: Lord of the Volcano
domains.subtitle: Wilderness, Desert, and Terrestrial Fire
domains.lead:
Aganjú is the orixá of the uninhabited places: volcanic earth, desert scrub, and the molten core beneath the mountain. Unlike Ṣàngó, whose fire crackles in the sky, Aganjú's fire moves slowly through stone. He is the son of Odùduwà and Ọbatalá in many accounts, the giant whose strides once shook the earth and whose breath still steams from fissures in the ground.

In Afro-Atlantic ritual he appears as Aggayú Solá, the bearer of the world, a deity so tall that rivers reach only his ankles. To invoke him is to acknowledge that civilization rests on forces older and more patient than human law.

cards.name: Volcanic Earth
cards.desc: Magma, lava fields, and earthquakes are his body; he is the planet's slow, burning voice.

cards.name: Desert Wilderness
cards.desc: The uninhabited plain where no farm can take root; the place beyond the town's edge.

cards.name: World-Bearer
cards.desc: In the diaspora he becomes the giant who supports the earth on his shoulders.

cards.name: Terrible Strength
cards.desc: Force without malice; the power that does not negotiate because it does not need to.

symbols.name: Volcanic stone
symbols.meaning: His seat and his bones; cooled lava is placed on altars to ground his presence.

symbols.name: Palm frond fan
symbols.meaning: Used to cool and direct his immense heat during ritual possession.

symbols.name: Red and brown beads
symbols.meaning: The colors of iron-rich earth, dried blood, and scorched clay.

symbols.name: Giant's staff
symbols.meaning: The walking stick of the world-bearer, marking his stride across deserts.

mythology.lead: Aganjú's myths are less numerous than those of Ọṣun or Ṣàngó, but they centre on a single theme: the earth as a living, burning body that carries human life without belonging to it. Where other orishas crowd the town and its markets, Aganjú's dossier is written at the boundary — volcano, desert, quarry — and in the diaspora's discovery that the wilderness god was carrying the world all along.

myths.title: Son of Odùduwà and Ọbatalá
myths.text: Aganjú's birth is a statement of his character: he arrives from the union of the two powers that divide the Yoruba cosmos. In many lineages he is counted a son of Odùduwà, the royal ancestor who founded the earth's cities, and of Ọbatalá, the white-clothed sculptor of human bodies; the genealogies vary — oral tradition keeps several versions, and no single Ifá corpus settles the question. What the variants agree on is the outcome. This child of kingship and craft refuses both inheritances and chooses the uncultivated bush, the lava field, the place no farm can claim. Where Ọbatalá shapes and Odùduwà rules, Aganjú simply burns and bears. Divination verses recorded by Bascom and others keep him at the world's edge, immense and mostly silent, invoked when the earth itself must be addressed — droughts, eruptions, the cracking of foundations. The myth means that every order rests on an unowned force it cannot command: the volcano is the family member the palace never invited home.

myths.title: The King Who Became the Volcano
myths.text: A second tradition makes Aganjú not a god from birth but a king who became one. Samuel Johnson's History of the Yorubas (1921), the great early record of Oyo tradition, preserves the memory of an Aláàfin — a king of the old Ọ̀yọ́ empire — remembered as Aganjú, whose rule ended in apotheosis: his name passed to the orisha of the wilderness, and the royal cult and the wilderness cult folded into one figure. Johnson is a single, late, colonial-era source, and modern scholarship treats the deified-king account cautiously — it may be a rationalization, or a genuinely remembered apotheosis of the kind Yoruba kingship often produced. But the tradition matters even if it is embroidery, because it explains why Aganjú carries both a king's gravity and a volcano's indifference to law. The myth means that the wilderness god may once have worn a crown — and that a king too fierce for the palace could still find a temple.

myths.title: Aggayú Solá Carries the World
myths.text: In Cuban Santería, Aganjú crosses the Atlantic and grows. As Aggayú Solá — the name already swelling with the sea-voyage — he is imagined as a giant so tall that rivers reach his ankles and palm trees are grass under his feet; he walks through lava as others walk through sand, and the earth rides on his shoulders like a load. When he possesses a devotee in ceremony, the person's whole gait changes: the step becomes heavy, swaying, patient, as if the ground under the dancer has remembered it is alive. Verger, who documented the orisha cults on both sides of the Atlantic, records that the diaspora re-centered Aganjú from the edge of settlement into the very center of the ritual house, pairing him with Ṣàngó as earth-fire to sky-fire. The transformation is the myth's meaning: a god of the uninhabited place became, in exile, the god who carries the inhabited one. The wilderness orisha ends up holding the whole world.

myths.title: The Desert and the Town
myths.text: Aganjú's cult geography is a map of the human boundary. His offerings — palm wine, smoked fish, red palm oil — are carried to the edge of towns, to road-cuts and quarries, to the last wall before the bush begins; in Candomblé houses his assentamento of iron-rich and volcanic stones sits low and grounded, as close to the floor as a god can get. Unlike Ọṣun, whose rivers run through the marketplace, Aganjú keeps the places where people stop and wilderness resumes. Mason's studies of New World Yoruba ritual describe the deliberate slowness of his rites: nothing about him is quick, because nothing about volcanoes is quick. The theology is stated by the offering site itself — civilization rests on older, hotter forces and owes them a share. The myth means that the wall around the city is a courtesy the wilderness extends, not a victory it has conceded.

lore.syncretism: In Brazilian Candomblé, Aganjú is syncretised with Saint Christopher, the giant who carries the Christ child across water. In Cuban Santería he becomes Aggayú Solá, often paired with the thunder-god Ṣàngó as complementary powers of sky-fire and earth-fire. The identification with Saint Christopher preserves the theme of colossal bearing strength, while the pairing with Ṣàngó maps the volcanic interior onto the stormy sky. Christianity gave him a new face but kept his scale.
lore.culturalLegacy: Aganjú remains one of the less domesticated orixás. He is not the god of the marketplace or the bedroom; he is the god of what lies beneath and beyond. In an age of ecological awareness, his mythology reads like a warning: the ground we build on is alive, slow, and capable of overwhelming any city. His colors — red, brown, and iron — appear in Candomblé and Santería altars, and his giant stride survives in the heavy, deliberate dance of his possessed devotees.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Aganjú teaches that stillness is not absence. The volcano sleeps for centuries; the desert seems empty; the earth beneath the pavement does not speak. And yet all of them hold forces that could reshape the world in a single day. Aganjú is the god of that withheld power.

To meditate on him is to remember that human institutions are thin crust on a molten sphere. He does not hate the city, but he does not need it. His gift is perspective: from the rim of a volcano or the centre of a desert, the anxieties of the town shrink to their proper size. He asks only that we do not mistake our maps for the territory.

lore.archaeology: Direct archaeological attestation of Aganjú is sparse because Yoruba orixá cults were transmitted orally and through ritual objects rather than temple inscriptions. In Yorubaland, volcanic-stone implements, iron slag from early smelting, and boundary markers in uncultivated bush mark the zones over which such wilderness orishas preside. The diaspora, by contrast, keeps a dense material record: the assentamento — the stone-and-metal altar of Candomblé houses — regularly includes volcanic and iron-bearing stones for Aganjú, his palm-frond fan, and beadwork in his red and brown colors. Cuban ilé-orishá shelves hold similar offerings, and chalk-drawn firmas diagram his volcano in Lucumí practice. The orisha who owns uncarved wilderness lives on in carved, kept, and beaded objects.
